Abstract: Extreme soil erosion and flooding of roads and properties from agricultural land have been reported in many areas of the United Kingdom. This article reports the impact of a major storm and soil erosion incident which occurred in the village of Ashow, Warwickshire, on 30 August 1996, where erosion rates on a 16ha field were found to be equivalent to circa. 5000 tonnes per square kilometre. Four groups of factors are considered in relation to the damage caused to roads and properties. These include the possible decrease in soil resistance to erosion due to continuous cultivation over many centuries; the removal of hedgerows; the way in which seed beds are prepared, and the timing of seed bed preparation in relation to the likelihood of autumn thunderstorms. Whilst flooding is regarded as an Act of God for insurance purposes, we argue that in specific instances erosion and flooding may be caused more by farming practice than by an Act of God, and that farmers need to be more aware of the likelihood of severe storms, should assess risks of erosion, and should adjust their practices accordingly.

Title: Experimental investigation of competition between forest herbs; [Eksperymentalne badania zdolności konkurencyjnej roślin leśnych]

Abstract: The beech (Fagus sylvalica L.) has a wide ecological range; it occurs in numerous plant communities which differ in floristic composition and in ecology. It is not clear yet which factors lead to such a floristic differences within beech forests. Why do Vaccinium myrtillus, Luzula albida, Deschampsia flexuosa grow together in one case, Dentaria ssp., Mercurialis perennis, Asperula odorata in another, Carex alba, Epipactis rubiginosa, Cephalanthera ssp. in still others? Why does the first group of species occupy acid soils, and the last neutral or even alkaline soils? This study attempts to distinguish between the degrees of influence abiotic factors and com petition have on the composition of various beech associations. A field experiment was started to demonstrate whether plants characterizing acidophilous beech forests (Deschampsia flexuosa (L.) Trin., Luzula albida (Hoffm.) DC, Carex pilosa Scop.) will grow in other beech associations e.g. on rendzina soils, and vice-vers, whether plants such as Mercurialis perennis L., Carex alba Scop., Asperula odorata L. species occurring in beech forests chiefly on brown soils and rendzinas can develop on acid brown soils with a raw humus layer. To investigate the part played by competition the author planted both pure (mono-specific) and mixed cultures of these six plants. Species were planted on plots chosen randomly and hedged off within beech forest-stands representing three beech associations. The natural herb layer was removed without damaging the humus layer and tree roots. The plants for each species were obtained from well-defined areas of up to several tens of sq. metres of known soil conditions and microclimate, where species developed strongly and multiplied vegetatively. The plants appeared genetically uniform. Chemical analyses of the leaves of each species were made (table 1). The initial assimilating surface of one average planted exemplar amounted to about 30 sq. centimetres; in Mercurialls perennis the assimilating surface was some four times greater. The plants were planted in autumn 1964 (in 1965 on plot C) in the following conditions: in Tilio-Fagetum on rendzina soil - plot A, in Melico-Fagelum luzuletosum, Carex pilosa variant (further called Carici pilosae-Fagetum for short) on an acid brown soil - plot B; and in Luzulo-Fagetum (Melamp. Fagetum) on an acid brown soil with raw humus - plot C. The plots are situated at an altitude of 470-490 metres above sealevel in Martinsberg forest near Baden (Kanton Aargau, Switzerland, 25 km NW from Zürich). The average total precipitation is about 1000 mm, and the mean yearly air temperature 8.5°C. Floristic composition, microclimate, and soils were analysed on the experimental plots. Some data are listed in table 2 and fig. 1. On each mono-specific plot were 84 plants when planted; each species in mixed cultures was represented by 28 plants. There were 225 sq. cm of soil per plant. Four replications were made. In all, more than 8200 plants were planted. The plots were hand weeded once or twice in a year. In autumn 1965 and 1966 an inventory of all living plants was made, leaves measured, vegetative stems counted as well as seeds, etc. Thanks to the existing correlations between leaf length and assimilating surface in most investigated species it was possible to compare the changes in their surface without damaging the plants. The results were diagrammed and are summarized in table 2. (fig. 4-6). The investigations show that development is slow in the forest where light is restricted and strong root competition exists. The growth and development of plants in pure cultures differs little from multi-specific cultures. Only Mercurialis perennis, and Asperula odorata to a lesser degree, grow better in Tilio-Fagetum in mixed then in pure cultures. All replanted species, except Deschampsia flexuosa transplanted into acid soil with raw humus, responded to this transplantation into different environmental conditions by reducing their assimilating surface. Deschampsia flexuosa disappeared almost completely in the Tilio-Fagetum association. This species grows well, multiplies vegetatively and produces seed on the remaining plots where it did not occur naturally. Mercurialis perennis cannot grow on an acid brown soil with a raw humus layer; it shows strong symptoms of chlorosis, and it sheds its leaves some three months earlier than in the environments occupied naturally. All the species continue to grow on the acid brown soil. The investigations made seem to indicate that a factor with a basic importance for the formation of at least some communities of the beech (Luzulo-Fagetum, Tilio-Fagetum) is mineral nitrogen and its form in the soil. Mineral nitrogen becomes, owing to the demand for nitrogen, the chief object of plant competition. Soil acidity is only one of the factors conditioning the distribution of plants and may serve as a good indicator of processes occurring in the soil. In an acidophilous beech forest, on acid brown soils, species assemble (Vaccinium myrtillus, Luzula albida, Deschampsia flexuosa) which can utilize ammonium nitrogen (NH4-N) better than nitrate nitrogen (NO3-N). In fertile beech forests those species congregate which can better utilize NO3-N. The last are also environments well provided in cations of calcium and magnesium as well as others which condition a neutral or slightly alkaline soil reaction. Such factors make possible the development of a nitrifying microflora and hence the provision of more NO3-N. A direct influence of abiotic factors prevents Deschampsia flexuosa from growing in the Tilio-Fagetum association, and Mercurialis perennis in the Luzulo-Fagelum association. In environments characterized by a similar type of nitrogen regime, of Ca and Mg supply, of soil reaction, etc. the plant species usually show a wide ecological range and their distribution is, to a considerable degree, the effect of interspecific competition. This appeared especially sharply in the example of pairs of species: Mercurialis perennis - Asperula odorata, and Deschampsia flexuosa - Vaccinium myrtillus. Asperula odorata in mono-specific culture developed best in an environment which in natural conditions and in mixed cultures was dominated by Mercurialis perennis. Deschampsia flexuosa grew abundantly and multiplied on acid brown soils where it was absent in nature and where the dominant species were Vaccinium myrtillus and Luzula albida. Title: Trapping adult Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus (Coleoptera: Curculionidae) with aquatic barrier traps

Abstract: The rice water weevil, Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus Kuschel, is a pest of rice in the seven rice producing states of the United States and several countries where it has been introduced. Carbofuran was used adequately for nearly 30 yr, but it is no longer registered for use in rice and has been replaced by λ-cyhalothrin (Karate) and diflubenzuron (Dimilin). The scouting methods for carbofuran were inadequate or too late in determining the need for insecticide applications of the newer insecticides. Therefore, a new population monitoring method was developed using a double-ended aquatic barrier trap. The trap function was based on weevil swimming behavior, and 16 barrier trap prototypes were tested on adult weevils, 22-23 July 1998, in a small bay of late planted rice. Adult means ± SE were 73.9 ± 9.4 per trap on 23 July 1998 and 54.4 ± 6.4 per trap on 24 July 1998. The core sample mean for this plot was 72.9 ± 7.0 larvae per core. The trap was tested in both commercial fields and early and late planted small bays in 1999. Larval weevil infestations ranged from moderate (near or slightly below the economic injury level (EIL) to high (62.8 per core). Regression analyses showed a significant correlation between adults captured in traps to subsequent larval density in field edges (r2 = 0.98) and field interiors (r2 = 0.92). For every 1.0 rice water weevil adult captured in barrier traps, a density of 1.2-2.8 larvae per core sample was predicted. The aquatic barrier traps caught adult weevils without lures. Trapping rice water weevil adults immediately after permanent flood in drill-seeded fields can be used to aid decision making for insecticide application in rice.

Abstract: Preliminary field evaluations for 162 species are reported. This work represents a portion of a team-oriented effort to develop new crops for American agriculture. These species are potential new oilseed sources of epoxy, crepenynic, erucic, and other fatty acids, and sources of seed gum, steroids, and pulp. Euphorbia lagascae and Cephalaria setosa show the most promise for crop development as epoxy acid sources, but both require substantial improvement through breeding. Crepis alpina, a small-seeded species with excellent seed retention, is the best prospect for providing an oil rich in crepenynic acid. A selection and breeding program is under way. None of the species tested as erucic acid sources equalled the crop potential of crambe and selected Brassicas. Briza spicata, a small, moderately productive grass, is the richest known source of glycolipids. B. spicata has been grown successfully as a winter annual at several locations. Earlier maturity and better seedling vigor is needed in Satureja hortensis, a source of oil similar to linseed oil. Xeranthemum annuum, an attractive, winter annual and everlasting, is very good agronomically, but the use of the oil with its mixture of several fatty acids is not economically favorable. Solanum khasianum shows agronomic promise as a source of the steroid, solasodine. Cassia occidentalis, C. bonariensis, Crotalaria leioloba, and C. stipularia are productive potential seed gum sources. These species, especially Cassia occidentalis, seem to be sufficiently good agronomically to justify intensive breeding. Of the various sources of pulp, emphasis is on kenaf because highyielding, well-adapted varieties are available. Crotalaria juncea merits breeding effort, and other species show sufficient promise for further evaluation. © 1971 The New York Botanical Garden.

Title: A four-year investigation into the efficacy of domiciles for enhancement of bumble bee populations

Abstract: 1 Eighty four-unit domiciles for introduced bumble bees (Bombus spp.) were placed in 16 field margins at Lincoln, New Zealand in the 1995-96 southern summer. Fifty-five were placed in the margins of intensively managed fields, with the remaining 25 being in less disturbed habitats, which had more spring/summer floral resources. 2 The number of nests founded over the four-year study period increased from one to 27. Bombus hortorum was a much more frequent colonist than was B. terrestris, with B. ruderatus colonizing only in the fourth year. 3 In the 'intensive' sites, mean four-year occupancy was only 2%, whereas in the less disturbed sites it was 13%. 4 There was a positive association between bumble bee occupancy of the domicile compartments in the previous year and occupancy in the current year. No association was found between previous occupancy by mice and subsequent occupancy by bumble bees. 5 The potential for adding Bombus nest sites to agricultural land to enhance local populations, and, potentially, pollination of seed crops, is discussed. Adding domiciles in intensively managed landscapes may not be very effective unless spring floral resources are enhanced as well.
